lab_title: AR Lab: Apparent Retrograde Motion of Mars (and Comparison to Jupiter & Saturn)
top_level_objectives: Explain why Mars shows apparent retrograde motion over weeks, including the role of relative motion between Earth and Mars.
Interpret observations from Earth’s viewpoint in terms of the heliocentric model.
Describe how the outer-planet retrograde loop arises when Earth overtakes a slower-moving outer planet on its orbit.
Compare retrograde behavior across Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn and connect differences to orbital speed and geometry.

scenes.scene_name: Scene 1 — The Night-Sky Puzzle (Mars Drifts, Then Loops)
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the observational pattern of apparent retrograde motion and frame the geocentric vs heliocentric explanation challenge.
key_visuals: A star field with constellations labeled
Mars plotted as a bright marker moving slowly eastward day-to-day
A timeline indicator showing “weeks” and the approximate moment retrograde begins
Optional overlay: arrow showing “normal eastward drift” transitioning into “westward loop”
student_actions: Observe the marker’s path and identify when Mars slows, stops, then reverses direction.
Mark (mentally or via a selection) the dates/intervals corresponding to the start of retrograde and the end of the loop.

scenes.scene_name: Scene 2 — Earth-Based Watching: Tracking Mars Across Constellations
scenes.brief_purpose: Have students practice reading sky observations: how retrograde appears against the fixed background of stars from a single vantage point.
key_visuals: AR view anchored to an implied observing location (horizon/sky dome)
Mars’s path projected across identifiable constellation shapes
A “direction” guide that flips from eastward to westward during retrograde
A simple scale bar for angular motion per week (relative, not exact units)
student_actions: Follow Mars along the constellation background and describe the apparent motion direction during three phases: pre-retrograde, retrograde, and post-retrograde.
Answer a quick prompt: “Which direction is Mars moving relative to the stars at this moment?” and “Is it actually moving backward in space?” (concept check).

scenes.scene_name: Scene 3 — Switch to the Heliocentric Model: Earth and Mars in Orbit
scenes.brief_purpose: Connect the sky observation to smooth orbital motion by shifting perspective to outside the solar system.
key_visuals: A viewpoint outside the solar system showing the Sun at the center
Two orbit tracks: Earth’s inner orbit and Mars’s outer orbit with planet icons
A time scrubber that advances days smoothly
Arrows or velocity indicators showing Earth moves faster than Mars
student_actions: Run the time progression through the period corresponding to Mars’s sky loop.
Predict what Earth and Mars are doing at the time Mars appears to slow and reverse (e.g., “Earth approaching/overtaking”).

scenes.scene_name: Scene 4 — Explain the Loop: Earth Overtakes Mars (Car-Passing Analogy)
scenes.brief_purpose: Make the causal mechanism explicit: the apparent loop is generated by relative motion along the line of sight, not by Mars changing its direction in space.
key_visuals: Earth and Mars positions at key moments: approach, closest approach (loop midpoint), and post-overtake
Line-of-sight arrows from the Sun/Earth system indicating relative angular change
A side-by-side comparison: left panel shows Earth’s sky view; right panel shows orbital positions
A “relative angular speed” indicator that peaks when Earth overtakes Mars
student_actions: Match three orbital moments to three sky-view moments on a short mapping task.
State the rule in their own words: retrograde occurs when Earth’s faster orbital motion reduces the line-of-sight angle, then increases it in the opposite sense.

scenes.scene_name: Scene 5 — Compare Planets: Why Jupiter and Saturn Loop Less
scenes.brief_purpose: Apply the same reasoning to other outer planets and relate loop size to orbital distance and relative speed.
key_visuals: Toggles for planet selection: Mars, Jupiter, Saturn
For each planet: orbital animations on the outside view
Overlay of each planet’s apparent path on the same sky background scale for comparison
Velocity/relative-motion notes: larger Sun-to-planet distance implies slower orbital speed
student_actions: Observe how the apparent retrograde loop amplitude and duration differ among Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
Choose the best explanation for the observed differences: relative-motion effect strength decreases for more distant planets.

scenes.scene_name: Scene 6 — Synthesis Check: From Observation to Explanation
scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate understanding by having students articulate the full observational-to-theoretical reasoning chain.
key_visuals: A summary diagram: Earth-based sky path (with loop) linked to heliocentric orbit geometry
A “cause-effect” flow visualization: Earth faster orbit → overtaking geometry → apparent retrograde loop
A final time-lapse freeze at the loop midpoint labeled clearly
student_actions: Write or select a short explanation describing what changes in the heliocentric model at the moment retrograde is greatest.
Complete a final comparison statement: “Mars shows a larger loop than Jupiter because ________.”
